title: Cultured Meat Economics (detailed)
body:
## What it is
Cultured (cell-cultivated) meat is real animal meat grown from animal cells in bioreactors instead of raised on a farm and slaughtered. This record examines the economics: what drives the cost per kilogram and what has to change for price parity with conventional meat.

## State of the art (2026)
As of 2026, cultivated meat is legally sold in only a few markets, including Singapore and the United States (where two companies received regulatory clearance in 2023). Production is at pilot scale, portions are small and expensive, and most products blend cultivated cells with plant protein to manage cost.

## Who is building it
Work is concentrated in food-tech startups and a handful of large meat and ingredient companies running pilot plants. Academic groups publish most of the open cost modeling, since company cost figures are rarely disclosed.

## How it works
A small biopsy of animal cells is expanded in a nutrient growth medium inside a stainless-steel bioreactor, similar to brewing. The cells are harvested, formed into a product, and finished like conventional meat. The dominant costs are the growth medium (especially growth factors), bioreactor capital, and energy.

## Honest timeline
Honest assessment: price parity with commodity ground meat is not expected this decade at current learning rates; premium products (nuggets, fillets sold at a premium) arrive first. Watch medium-cost reduction and bioreactor scale-up, not announcements.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.
demo_code:
"""Demo for "Cultured Meat Economics (detailed)": Wright's-law learning curve. Executed at build time."""
C0, PR = 325000, 0.8  # starting cost, progress ratio per doubling
DOUBLINGS = [1, 3, 5, 8, 10]; TARGET = 10
LABEL = 'cultivated burger cost (2013 lab burger ~$325k)'; UNIT = '$/kg-equivalent'
print("=" * 64)
print("LEARNING CURVE (Wright's law):", LABEL)
print(f"Start: {C0} {UNIT}; progress ratio {PR} per cumulative doubling")
print("-" * 64)
for d in DOUBLINGS:
    c = C0 * (PR ** d)
    flag = "  <-- at/below target" if c <= TARGET else ""
    print(f"  after {d:2d} doublings: {c:>12,.2f} {UNIT}{flag}")
print("-" * 64)
import math
need = math.log(TARGET / C0) / math.log(PR) if TARGET < C0 else 0
print(f"Doublings needed to reach {TARGET} {UNIT}: {need:.1f}")
assert 0 < PR < 1 and C0 > 0
demo_output:

Start: 325000 $/kg-equivalent; progress ratio 0.8 per cumulative doubling

  after  3 doublings:   166,400.00 $/kg-equivalent
  after  5 doublings:   106,496.00 $/kg-equivalent
  after  8 doublings:    54,525.95 $/kg-equivalent

title: Digital Twins of Cities (history)
body:
## What it is
A digital twin of a city is a living software model of the urban environment: streets, buildings, traffic, energy, water, and people flows, kept in sync with sensor data. This record traces the idea from early 3D city models to today's real-time urban twins.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, major cities operate digital twins for traffic management, flood modeling, and planning approval. The models combine GIS, building information models, and live feeds from traffic cameras, transit systems, and utilities. Full closed-loop control (the twin issuing commands back to the city) remains rare.

## Who is building it
City governments, national mapping agencies, and large engineering software vendors build the platforms. Research groups publish the standards work that lets different cities' models interoperate.

## How it works
Static geometry (from lidar scans and building plans) is fused with live sensor streams into one model. Simulation engines then forecast congestion, emissions, or flood spread hours ahead. Planners test interventions in the twin before touching the real street.

## Honest timeline
Already deployed for planning and monitoring; the honest frontier is automated control and cross-city twins, which need better data standards and governance more than new algorithms.

## Feasibility
BUILDABLE NOW — deployed or commercially available in 2026; remaining challenges are cost, scale, and adoption, not feasibility.
demo_code:
"""Demo for "Digital Twins of Cities (history)": scaling estimate. Executed at build time."""
TARGET = 10000  # cities with >100k people worldwide (~10,000)
UNIT_CAP = 250  # city twins a large vendor can onboard per year
UNIT = 'twins/year'
print("=" * 64)
print("SCALING ESTIMATE")
need = TARGET / UNIT_CAP
print(f"  Target: {TARGET:,}")
print(f"  Unit capacity: {UNIT_CAP:,} {UNIT}")
print(f"  Units required: {need:,.1f}")
print(f"  Years at 1x unit rate: {need:,.1f}; at 10x: {need/10:,.1f}")
print("=" * 64)
assert need > 0

title: Autonomous Everything (overview)
body:
## What it is
Autonomy is the migration of driving, flying, warehouse work, farming, and inspection from human operators to machines that perceive, decide, and act. This overview maps where autonomy actually works in 2026 and where it is still a research project.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026 autonomy is real in bounded domains: robotaxis operate commercially in several cities, warehouse robots are standard in large fulfillment centers, and agricultural autosteer is decades old. Unbounded open-road full autonomy and general-purpose humanoids remain research-stage.

## Who is building it
Vehicle makers, dedicated AV companies, logistics firms, and farm equipment manufacturers. Regulators in the US, EU, China, and Japan set the operating envelopes.

## How it works
The standard stack is perception (cameras, lidar, radar fused), prediction of other actors, planning, and control, trained on fleet data and simulation. Safety is argued through redundancy, operational design domains, and disengagement statistics.

## Honest timeline
Expect autonomy to keep winning bounded domains first (highways, campuses, warehouses, mines). Open-world everywhere autonomy has no credible arrival date; treat vendor timelines with skepticism.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.
demo_code:
"""Demo for "Autonomous Everything (overview)": timeline projection (compound growth model). Executed at build time."""
Y0, V0, RATE = 2026, 700000, 0.6
YEARS = [2027, 2028, 2030, 2032, 2035]
LABEL = 'autonomous rides per week (illustrative, all operators)'; UNIT = 'rides/week'
print("=" * 64)
print("TIMELINE PROJECTION:", LABEL)
print(f"Base: {V0} {UNIT} in {Y0}; annual rate {RATE:+.1%}")
print("-" * 64)
for y in YEARS:
    v = V0 * (1 + RATE) ** (y - Y0)
    print(f"  {y}: {v:,.2f} {UNIT}")
print("-" * 64)
print("Model: compound growth from a real base figure; extrapolation, not prediction.")
assert all(isinstance(y, int) for y in YEARS)

title: Brain-Computer Interfaces Go Mainstream (overview)
body:
## What it is
Brain-computer interfaces translate neural activity into control signals for computers, prosthetics, or communication devices. This overview covers the path from clinical implants to consumer headsets.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, implanted BCIs remain clinical: a small number of human trial participants control cursors and robotic arms, and speech-decoding from cortical implants has been demonstrated in research. Non-invasive EEG headsets are consumer products but offer low bandwidth (a few reliable commands).

## Who is building it
Clinical trials run at universities and a few well-funded neurotech companies; consumer EEG is a crowded gadget market. Regulators treat implants as high-risk medical devices.

## How it works
Electrodes record neural firing; decoders (increasingly neural networks) map patterns to intended movement or speech. Implants trade surgical risk for signal quality; scalp EEG trades safety for a blurry, slow signal.

## Honest timeline
Clinical communication aids for locked-in patients are the near term and already partly here. Mainstream consumer thought-control is not on any credible near-term roadmap; the signal physics is the bottleneck.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Molecular Assemblers (applications)
body:
## What it is
Molecular assemblers are the hypothesized machines of nanotechnology's founding vision: devices that build products atom by atom, placing each molecule where a blueprint says. This record surveys the proposed applications, from desktop manufacturing to medicine.

## State of the art (2026)
As of 2026, no molecular assembler exists and no laboratory has demonstrated positional assembly of arbitrary molecules. Real nanotechnology works differently: DNA origami, scanning-probe manipulation of single atoms, and self-assembly. The assembler remains a concept with detailed designs but no build path.

## Who is building it
The concept lives in futurist literature and a small academic community; mainstream nanotechnology funding goes to self-assembly, DNA nanotech, and advanced materials.

## How it works
In the vision, a feedstock of reactive molecules is positioned by nanoscale manipulators under computer control, forming covalent bonds at chosen sites, with error correction borrowed from biology's ribosomes. Every step of this chain is currently beyond reach.

## Honest timeline
No credible timeline exists. Treat any date attached to molecular assemblers as fiction; the honest statement is that we do not know how to build one.

## Feasibility
THEORETICAL — a concept or design with no working prototype path; honestly a design study or thought experiment, not an engineering program.

LABEL = 'atoms in a 1-gram product vs assembly rate'

print("PHYSICS CHECK:", LABEL)

title: Autonomous Everything (applications)
body:
## What it is
Where autonomy is actually applied today: the catalog of domains where machines already do the driving, flying, picking, spraying, or inspecting, and what each application demands.

## State of the art (2026)
Deployed applications in 2026 include highway truck autonomy pilots, mining haul trucks (autonomous for over a decade), warehouse mobile robots, crop-spraying drones, and infrastructure inspection drones. Each works because its domain is bounded and mapped.

## Who is building it
Mining companies, logistics operators, farm equipment makers, and drone service firms are the real deployers; the research frontier is handled by AV and robotics labs.

## How it works
Every application follows the same recipe: constrain the environment, map it exhaustively, instrument the machine with redundant sensing, and keep a human fallback or a safe-stop behavior. Applications fail when the environment is allowed to surprise the machine.

## Honest timeline
Applications expand domain by domain, not all at once. The next wins are ports, campuses, and fixed-route freight; the last wins are chaotic urban mixed traffic.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Autonomous Everything (faq)
body:
## What it is
Frequently asked questions about autonomy, answered plainly: safety, jobs, liability, timelines, and what 'self-driving' actually means.

## State of the art (2026)
Public understanding lags deployment: driver-assist systems are routinely mistaken for self-driving, and every high-profile crash resets the debate. Regulators in 2026 distinguish clearly between driver support (human responsible) and automated driving (system responsible within its domain).

## Who is building it
Safety agencies, insurers, and consumer groups shape the answers as much as the technology companies do.

## How it works
Answers rest on three facts: the operational design domain (where the system is allowed to work), the fallback behavior (what it does when confused), and the safety case (the evidence it is at least as safe as a human in that domain).

## Honest timeline
The FAQ never expires: each newly automated domain replays the same questions. Expect the liability question to stay open longest.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: De-Extinction Projects (overview)
body:
## What it is
De-extinction aims to bring back extinct species, or functional proxies of them, using ancient DNA, gene editing, and surrogate mothers. This overview separates the science from the spectacle.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026 no extinct species has been revived. Companies and labs have announced edited embryos and pups with some mammoth or dire-wolf traits gestated in living relatives, but these are trait-edited modern animals, not resurrected species. Woolly mammoth work centers on editing elephant cells with mammoth traits like cold tolerance.

## Who is building it
A few well-funded startups lead the publicity; ancient-DNA labs at universities and museums supply the genomes. Conservation biologists are split on whether the money should go to living endangered species.

## How it works
Ancient DNA is sequenced from fossils, compared against the closest living relative's genome, and key differences are edited into living cells with CRISPR. Edited embryos would be carried by surrogate mothers of the living species. Each step works in isolation; the chain has not produced a viable proxy population.

## Honest timeline
Trait-edited animals within years; self-sustaining proxy populations, if ever, are decades out and face ecological and ethical barriers bigger than the technical ones.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Smart Dust Sensors (examples)
body:
## What it is
Smart dust is the vision of millimeter-scale wireless sensors scattered by the thousands to monitor environments, structures, or bodies. This record collects concrete example deployments and prototypes.

## State of the art (2026)
True dust-sized autonomous sensors do not exist in 2026. What exists: grain-of-rice-sized prototypes in labs, cubic-millimeter wireless sensor motes demonstrated in research, and practical 'smart dust adjacent' deployments of small wireless sensors for agriculture and infrastructure monitoring.

## Who is building it
University sensor labs and a few startups; the volume business is in larger industrial wireless sensors from established vendors.

## How it works
The physics squeeze is power: a millimeter mote cannot carry a battery, so designs harvest vibration, light, or RF energy and communicate by backscatter. Sensing, computing, and radio must all fit in microwatts.

## Honest timeline
Infrastructure monitoring with small (not dust) sensors is here. Dust-scale autonomy waits on energy harvesting and remains a lab pursuit.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Space-Based Solar Power (examples)
body:
## What it is
Collecting sunlight in orbit, where it never sets and never passes through clouds, and beaming the energy to Earth. This record lists the concrete demonstration projects.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026 space solar power is at the demonstration stage: small orbital experiments have beamed modest power wirelessly over short distances, and ground rectenna tests have received beamed microwave power. No system delivers grid power; the economics are dominated by launch cost.

## Who is building it
Space agencies in the US, Europe, Japan, and China run the demo programs; launch providers set the cost floor that determines viability.

## How it works
Photovoltaic arrays in geostationary orbit collect ~13x the annual energy per panel of a cloudy ground site, convert it to microwaves or laser, and beam it to a large ground rectenna that converts it back to electricity. End-to-end efficiency and beam safety are the engineering questions.

## Honest timeline
Demonstrations this decade; grid contribution only if launch costs fall another order of magnitude and kilometer-scale assembly in orbit is proven. Treat 2040s grid claims as aspirational.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Artificial General Intelligence (examples)
body:
## What it is
AGI means machine intelligence that matches or exceeds humans across essentially all cognitive work, not just one task. This record collects what 'examples' of progress toward AGI actually look like versus what is claimed.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, large AI models show broad capabilities across language, code, and some reasoning benchmarks, but they remain unreliable at long-horizon planning, true causal understanding, and autonomous real-world action. No system meets any serious definition of AGI; experts disagree wildly on timelines, from years to never.

## Who is building it
A handful of large AI labs and the cloud providers that fund them; academic researchers probe capabilities and failure modes.

## How it works
Current systems learn statistical patterns from vast data and predict likely continuations. Proposed paths to generality include better reasoning architectures, embodied learning in robots, and neurosymbolic hybrids. None is proven.

## Honest timeline
No credible consensus date exists. Honest framing: capabilities keep broadening, reliability keeps lagging, and 'AGI arrival' will likely be recognized in hindsight, if at all.

## Feasibility
BREAKTHROUGH-DEPENDENT — practical deployment needs at least one major scientific or engineering breakthrough beyond steady incremental progress.

title: Thought-Controlled Devices (detailed)
body:
## What it is
Devices operated directly by decoded neural intent: wheelchairs, cursors, prosthetic limbs, and communication aids driven by thought rather than muscle. A detailed look at the signal chain.

## State of the art (2026)
Clinical implants let paralyzed users type at tens of words per minute via decoded attempted handwriting and control robotic arms. Non-invasive systems manage simple selections. The gap between lab demos and reliable daily use is signal stability over months.

## Who is building it
Neurotech trial sponsors, rehabilitation hospitals, and university brain-machine labs.

## How it works
Electrodes sample neural activity; a decoder trained on calibration data maps firing patterns to intended actions; the device executes with smoothing and error correction. Performance degrades as scar tissue forms or electrodes drift, requiring recalibration.

## Honest timeline
Assistive communication for paralysis is the real near term. Consumer thought control waits on non-invasive bandwidth physics that has not budged in decades.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Anti-Aging Breakthroughs (faq)
body:
## What it is
Can aging be slowed, stopped, or reversed? Plain answers to the most asked questions about longevity science.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, no intervention is proven to extend healthy human lifespan. Rapamycin, metformin, and senolytics show lifespan effects in mice; human trials target age-related diseases, not aging itself. Partial cellular reprogramming rejuvenates cells in animals but is far from a therapy.

## Who is building it
Longevity biotech startups, aging-research institutes, and the clinical trial networks testing candidates against specific diseases.

## How it works
The leading strategies: clear senescent cells, reprogram aged cells toward youth, replace aged blood factors, and target the hallmarks of aging (genomic instability, epigenetic drift, mitochondrial decline). Each works partially in animals; human translation is the graveyard of mouse cures.

## Honest timeline
Expect better treatments for age-related diseases first; validated human lifespan extension, if possible, is decades of trials away. Anyone selling it now is selling hope.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Fusion Power Timelines (overview)
body:
## What it is
Fusion promises near-limitless clean energy from seawater fuel. This overview tracks why the timeline keeps slipping and what would actually constitute arrival.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, fusion has achieved scientific breakeven: the US National Ignition Facility demonstrated net energy gain from a fusion reaction (2022, repeated since), and private fusion companies have raised billions. No device produces net electricity; the best tokamaks are large international projects running years behind schedule.

## Who is building it
National labs, the ITER project in France, and a crowded field of private fusion startups pursuing tokamaks, stellarators, and inertial approaches.

## How it works
Magnetic confinement (tokamaks, stellarators) holds hot plasma in magnetic bottles; inertial confinement crushes fuel pellets with lasers. Both must simultaneously achieve temperature, density, and confinement time, then convert heat to electricity economically.

## Honest timeline
First net-electricity demonstrations are plausible in the 2030s; grid-relevant fusion power is a 2040s-or-later story. The honest milestone to watch is a device sustaining net electricity, not press-release plasma records.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

## What it is
Growing transplantable organs from a patient's own cells would end the organ shortage and rejection. This record surveys the applications closest to reality.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, lab-grown simple tissues are clinical reality: skin, cartilage, and bioengineered blood vessels are used in patients. Bladders and windpipes have been implanted experimentally. Complex vascularized organs (liver, kidney, heart) remain research-stage; whole-organ transplants from bioprinting have not happened.

## Who is building it
Tissue-engineering labs, regenerative-medicine companies, and transplant centers running early trials.

## How it works
Patient cells are seeded onto biodegradable scaffolds shaped like the target tissue and matured in bioreactors that mimic the body's mechanical and chemical cues. Vascularization (growing the blood-vessel plumbing) is the unsolved core problem for thick organs.

## Honest timeline
Simple tissues now; hollow organs in trials this decade; solid vascularized organs are a 2040s question at best. No manufacturing instructions are given here; this is a reference overview.

title: Molecular Assemblers (overview)
body:
## What it is
The founding concept of nanotechnology: programmable machines that build with atomic precision. This overview covers the idea, the famous debate, and why mainstream nanotech went a different way.

## State of the art (2026)
The concept was detailed in the 1980s-90s literature; a famous exchange between its chief proponent and a Nobel chemist ended with the mainstream view that chemistry doesn't work like tiny factories. Modern nanotech builds via self-assembly and DNA origami instead. No assembler program exists at any major lab.

## Who is building it
A small community keeps the design literature alive; the funding and results are in self-assembly, nanoporous materials, and DNA nanotechnology.

## How it works
The imagined mechanism: computer-controlled molecular manipulators performing mechanosynthesis (forming bonds by mechanical positioning). Critics note the 'fat fingers' problem (manipulators are themselves molecular and sticky) and the 'sticky fingers' problem; proponents have published rebuttal designs. The debate is philosophical without an experiment to settle it.

## Honest timeline
There is no experimental program converging on an assembler, so there is no timeline. It remains a design concept, honestly labeled theoretical.

## Feasibility
THEORETICAL — a concept or design with no working prototype path; honestly a design study or thought experiment, not an engineering program.

The small design community and the chemists who critique the assumptions.

**THOUGHT EXPERIMENT** — this record is speculative and inconsistent with current physics. It is presented for imagination and discussion, never as working physics or engineering.

## What it is
Technology that controls gravity: artificial gravity without rotation, gravity shielding, or propulsion without propellant.

## State of the art (2026)
THOUGHT EXPERIMENT. No experiment has ever manipulated gravity beyond general relativity's predictions, and GR says gravity is spacetime curvature, not a force with a dial. Every 'gravity control' claim in history has failed replication. This record is speculation, never working physics.

## Who is building it
No legitimate research program; the topic lives in fringe literature and science fiction.

## How it works
There is no known mechanism: GR offers no coupling by which electromagnetism or any lab-accessible field alters spacetime curvature at useful scales. Proposed schemes contradict tested physics.

## Honest timeline

title: The Interplanetary Internet
body:
## What it is
Networking across the solar system: protocols that work when the speed of light makes every message take minutes to hours.

## State of the art (2026)
The core protocol (Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking, DTN) exists and has flown in tests; Mars orbiters already relay data with store-and-forward behavior. What's missing is the infrastructure: relay satellites, ground stations, and standards for a real solar-system network.

## Who is building it
Space agencies' networking teams and the standards groups.

## How it works
DTN replaces TCP's chatty handshakes with bundle protocols that tolerate long delays and blackouts. Nodes store data and forward when links appear. It's the postal service model instead of the telephone model.

## Honest timeline
Mars relay networking this decade as traffic grows; a true interplanetary internet follows human presence, not precedes it.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: The Longevity Escape
body:
## What it is
Longevity escape velocity: the idea that medicine will soon extend life faster than time passes, making the first immortal generation already alive.

## State of the art (2026)
The concept is a thought experiment from the 2000s, not a research program. No data supports an approaching escape: human lifespan gains have slowed in wealthy countries, and no intervention extends healthy human lifespan. The idea survives as motivation, not as science.

## Who is building it
The concept's originators and the demographers tracking the actual curves.

## How it works
The mechanism would require each decade of medical progress to add more than a decade of life expectancy — a compounding that has never been observed. Actual gains come in shrinking increments as easy wins (sanitation, antibiotics) are exhausted.

## Honest timeline
No evidence-based timeline; the honest demography points to incremental gains.

## Feasibility
BREAKTHROUGH-DEPENDENT — practical deployment needs at least one major scientific or engineering breakthrough beyond steady incremental progress.

title: Solid-State Batteries
body:
## What it is
Batteries with solid electrolytes instead of flammable liquid: safer, denser, and the industry's most-wanted breakthrough.

## State of the art (2026)
In 2026, solid-state batteries are in the pilot-production phase: automakers and battery firms run pilot lines, and limited products (some consumer electronics, early EV deployments) exist. Mass EV adoption is not here; manufacturing at scale with acceptable yield and cost remains the industry's central challenge.

## Who is building it
Major automakers, Korean and Japanese battery giants, Chinese leaders, and a field of startups, all racing pilot lines.

## How it works
A ceramic or sulfide solid electrolyte replaces the liquid, enabling lithium-metal anodes for higher energy density and removing flammability. The manufacturing challenges are interfacial resistance, dendrite penetration through the solid, and pressure/temperature control in production.

## Honest timeline
Pilot production now; mass-market EVs on solid-state are a late-2020s to 2030s story if yields cooperate. Watch shipped volumes, not announcements.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

print(f"Start: {C0} {UNIT}; progress ratio {PR} per cumulative doubling")
print("-" * 64)
for d in DOUBLINGS:

    flag = "  <-- at/below target" if c <= TARGET else ""
    print(f"  after {d:2d} doublings: {c:>12,.2f} {UNIT}{flag}")

import math

print(f"Doublings needed to reach {TARGET} {UNIT}: {need:.1f}")
assert 0 < PR < 1 and C0 > 0

## What it is
Batteries pairing lithium with sulfur cathodes: far higher theoretical energy density than lithium-ion, at potentially lower cost.

## State of the art (2026)
Lithium-sulfur is a perennial lab star: energy densities multiples of lithium-ion are demonstrated, but cycle life (the polysulfide shuttle dissolving the cathode) has kept it out of products for decades. In 2026, niche applications (drones, high-altitude aircraft) see limited use; EVs do not.

The research groups and the startups targeting aerospace niches where cycle life matters less.

## Honest timeline
Niche aerospace now; mainstream use awaits a cycle-life solution that has been 'five years away' for twenty years.

title: Sodium-Ion Batteries
body:
## What it is
Batteries using sodium instead of lithium: cheaper materials, no lithium supply constraints, slightly lower performance.

## State of the art (2026)
Sodium-ion reached early commercialization by 2026: major Chinese manufacturers ship sodium-ion cells for stationary storage and low-cost EVs, and two-wheelers. Energy density trails lithium-ion, but cost and material abundance are the selling points.

## Who is building it
Chinese battery leaders first to market, with Korean and Western firms developing their own chemistries.

## How it works
Sodium ions shuttle like lithium ions but are larger and heavier, costing energy density. The win is materials: sodium is abundant everywhere, and cathodes can avoid nickel and cobalt.

## Honest timeline
Commercial now for storage and budget EVs; the question is how far up the performance ladder it climbs.

title: Iron-Air Batteries
body:
## What it is
Batteries that store energy by rusting and un-rusting iron: extremely cheap materials for multi-day grid storage.

## State of the art (2026)
Iron-air is in the demonstration phase: a well-known US startup is building its first commercial-scale factory for long-duration storage, with utility pilots. The chemistry is a century old (Edison's nickel-iron era); the innovation is making it cheap and reversible enough for the grid.

## Who is building it
The long-duration storage startup(s), utilities buying multi-day storage, and DOE demonstration funding.

## How it works
Discharge oxidizes iron (rusting), releasing electrons; charging reverses it. The materials cost almost nothing; the trade-offs are low round-trip efficiency and slow response, acceptable for storage measured in days.

## Honest timeline
First commercial deployments mid-2020s; the verdict comes from years of utility operating data.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Structural Batteries
body:
## What it is
Batteries that are also the structure: car body panels, aircraft wings, or phone frames that store energy while bearing load.

## State of the art (2026)
Research-stage in 2026: lab demonstrators show carbon-fiber composites that store charge, but the multifunctional trade-off is brutal — good batteries are bad structures and vice versa. No commercial structural battery product exists.

## Who is building it
The composites-and-electrochemistry research groups, mostly in Europe.

## How it works
Carbon fibers serve as both reinforcement and electrodes, with a structural electrolyte binding them. The design problem is Pareto: optimizing for both functions gives a mediocre battery and a mediocre structure; the win must come from system-level mass savings.

## Honest timeline
Lab demonstrators now; a product needs a vehicle program willing to accept the trade, likely 2030s if ever.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

title: Quantum Batteries (Theory)
body:
## What it is
The theoretical idea that quantum effects (entanglement, collective coupling) could let batteries charge faster than classical limits allow.

## State of the art (2026)
Pure theory: papers show quantum speedups in charging power for idealized models, but the models assume conditions (isolated systems, perfect control) that don't survive contact with real batteries. No experiment shows a useful quantum battery; the field is physics, not engineering.

## Who is building it
The quantum thermodynamics theorists.

## How it works
The claimed mechanism: N quantum cells charged collectively can absorb energy faster than N charged separately (superextensive scaling). The catch: decoherence destroys the effect at macroscopic scales and room temperature, which is where batteries live.

## Honest timeline
No timeline; honestly labeled theoretical, possibly forever.

## Feasibility
THEORETICAL — a concept or design with no working prototype path; honestly a design study or thought experiment, not an engineering program.

title: Flow Batteries for the Grid
body:
## What it is
Batteries that store energy in liquid electrolytes in external tanks: power and energy scale independently, ideal for multi-hour grid storage.

## State of the art (2026)
Commercial in 2026: vanadium redox flow batteries are deployed at grid scale (hundreds of MWh installations, especially in China), and zinc-bromine and iron-based variants compete. The technology works; the competition is lithium-ion's falling cost.

## Who is building it
The flow-battery vendors and the utilities buying long-duration storage.

## How it works
Two electrolyte tanks pump through a cell stack; capacity is tank size, power is stack size. Vanadium's advantage is using the same element both sides (no cross-contamination); its disadvantage is vanadium price volatility.

## Honest timeline
Deployed now for 4-12 hour storage; growth depends on beating lithium-ion on total cost for long durations.

## Feasibility

## What it is
Storing energy as heat in sand, brick, or molten salt: the cheapest possible storage for heat and, via heat engines, electricity.

## State of the art (2026)
Deployed in 2026: a commercial sand battery operates in Finland storing wind energy as heat for district heating, and brick-based industrial heat storage serves factories. As electricity storage (heat back to power) the round-trip efficiency is poor; as heat storage it's excellent and cheap.

The Nordic operators, industrial-heat startups, and the concentrated-solar plants that pioneered molten salt.

Resistive heaters or heat exchangers charge a well-insulated mass of sand or brick to hundreds of degrees; heat is withdrawn for buildings or industry. The economics work because the storage medium is nearly free.

Heat storage: commercial now. Heat-to-power: limited by thermodynamics to niche roles.

title: Gravity Batteries Revisited
body:
## What it is
Storing energy by lifting mass and releasing it by letting it fall: from ancient pumped hydro to modern gravity towers.

## State of the art (2026)
Pumped hydro is the world's dominant grid storage (over 90% of installed storage energy) and decades old. The 'revisited' part — lifting concrete blocks in towers or mineshafts — has pilot projects but no commercial fleet; the physics is unassailable and the economics are site-specific.

## Who is building it
The pumped-hydro operators, the gravity-tower startups, and mine owners with deep shafts.

## How it works
Energy stored is mgh: mass times height. Pumped hydro uses water and mountains; towers use blocks and cranes; mineshafts use weights in existing holes. Efficiency is good (75-85%); the constraint is finding cheap height and mass.

## Honest timeline
Pumped hydro: mature. Novel gravity: pilots now, commercial where geography cooperates.

Using hydrogen as the storage medium: electrolyze water when power is cheap, store the hydrogen, burn it or fuel-cell it back when power is dear.

## State of the art (2026)

The electrolyzer makers, gas utilities repurposing infrastructure, and heavy industry.

## Who is building it
The neural-interface labs and the prosthetics makers integrating feedback.

## How it works
Sensors in the prosthetic hand drive stimulators on residual nerves (implanted) or skin (non-invasive), creating referred sensations in the phantom hand. The brain learns the mapping with training.

## Honest timeline
Non-invasive now; implanted feedback in trials, expanding as interfaces improve.

## What it is
The carbon-fiber running prosthesis that turned amputee sprinting into a spectacle and a controversy.

## State of the art (2026)
Established technology in 2026: blades are standard Paralympic equipment, with decades of refinement. The controversy (do blades confer advantage?) was studied extensively; the consensus is they don't outperform biological legs overall. The engineering is mature.

Production by swarms of small robots instead of fixed lines: the factory floor as a colony.

## State of the art (2026)
Research and early pilots in 2026: swarm robotics is proven in labs and in warehouse robots (which are effectively swarms); manufacturing swarms that assemble products are experimental. The control and reliability questions are open.

The swarm-robotics labs and the logistics companies running the closest real thing.

Warehouses now (the proving ground); manufacturing swarms are a 2030s research bet.

title: The Biofactory
body:
## What it is
Factories that grow products: engineered microbes and cells manufacturing materials, chemicals, and food.

## State of the art (2026)
Real and growing in 2026: precision fermentation makes food proteins and materials; engineered yeast brews fragrances and pharmaceuticals; mycelium grows packaging and leather alternatives. The biofactory is commercial where biology beats chemistry on cost or novelty.

## Who is building it
The synbio foundries and the brands buying bio-made ingredients.

## How it works
Engineered organisms convert feedstocks in fermenters; downstream processing purifies the product. Scale-up is the discipline: what works in a flask must survive a 100,000-liter tank.

## Honest timeline
Commercial now in ingredients and materials; expanding as strain engineering and fermentation economics improve.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.
demo_code:
"""Demo for "The Biofactory": Wright's-law learning curve. Executed at build time."""
C0, PR = 1000, 0.8  # starting cost, progress ratio per doubling
DOUBLINGS = [1, 2, 3, 4]; TARGET = 50
LABEL = 'precision-fermentation ingredient cost'; UNIT = '$/kg (illustrative bio-ingredient)'
print("=" * 64)
print("LEARNING CURVE (Wright's law):", LABEL)
print(f"Start: {C0} {UNIT}; progress ratio {PR} per cumulative doubling")
print("-" * 64)
for d in DOUBLINGS:
    c = C0 * (PR ** d)
    flag = "  <-- at/below target" if c <= TARGET else ""
    print(f"  after {d:2d} doublings: {c:>12,.2f} {UNIT}{flag}")
print("-" * 64)
import math
need = math.log(TARGET / C0) / math.log(PR) if TARGET < C0 else 0
print(f"Doublings needed to reach {TARGET} {UNIT}: {need:.1f}")
assert 0 < PR < 1 and C0 > 0

## What it is
Motors inside the wheels: no drivetrain, perfect torque vectoring, and new packaging freedom.

## State of the art (2026)
Early commercial in 2026: in-wheel motors power some commercial vehicles and appear in EV concepts; startups supply the technology. The challenges are unsprung mass (motors in wheels hurt ride and handling) and durability in the harsh wheel environment.

The motor startups and the commercial-vehicle adopters.

Each wheel gets its own motor, enabling independent torque control. The engineering fight is keeping motor mass low and sealing against water, dust, and shock.

Niche commercial now; passenger-car adoption needs the unsprung-mass problem solved convincingly.

## What it is
Batteries shuttling magnesium ions instead of lithium: divalent chemistry promising higher volumetric density.

## State of the art (2026)
Research stage in 2026: decades of work, no commercial cell. Magnesium's divalency (two electrons per ion) is the prize; the curse is sluggish ion movement and electrolyte incompatibility. The field advances slowly.

The persistent research groups and the automakers watching from a distance.

Mg2+ carries twice the charge per ion, promising compact storage; but the strong charge makes ions stick in host materials, killing kinetics. Electrolytes that plate magnesium reversibly without corroding everything are the hunt.

## Honest timeline
No commercial horizon; the honest label is long-term research.

body:
## What it is
The salt flats of Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia: the geography of the battery age's key metal.

## State of the art (2026)
Real and consequential in 2026: the Triangle supplies a large share of the world's lithium from brine evaporation; Chile and Argentina produce at scale, Bolivia's vast resources remain largely undeveloped. The producing countries, the miners, the battery makers, and the local communities.

## What it is
The frontier view of solid-state batteries: what the next wave of the technology promises beyond the current pilot phase. (Companion to JAH-FUT-TECH-000097; kept as a distinct record per the build brief.)

## State of the art (2026)
Frontier status 2026: beyond today's pilot lines, research targets lithium-metal anodes with sulfide and oxide electrolytes, dry-electrode manufacturing, and anode-free designs. The frontier questions are yield at gigafactory scale and cost below $100/kWh.

The same automakers, battery giants, and startups as the main record, plus the equipment makers whose dry-coating machines are the frontier bottleneck.

Frontier approaches: sulfide electrolytes for conductivity, oxide for stability, hybrid polymer-ceramic composites, and manufacturing borrowed from semiconductor and capacitor industries. Each path trades performance against manufacturability.

The frontier outlook: pilot volumes late 2020s, gigafactory scale only if dry manufacturing and yields deliver — a 2030s verdict.

## State of the art (2026)
Lab records in 2026 exceed 33% efficiency for perovskite-silicon tandems; pilot production begins; the blocker is stability (perovskites degrade with heat, moisture, and light). The efficiency is proven; the 25-year lifetime is not.

## Who is building it
The solar research labs, the tandem startups, and the established manufacturers watching.

## How it works
Perovskites' tunable bandgap harvests high-energy photons atop silicon's infrared harvest. The manufacturing promise is cheap solution processing; the reality must survive decades outdoors.

## Honest timeline
Pilot products late 2020s; the stability verdict decides whether tandems take the market in the 2030s.

## Feasibility
RESEARCH STAGE — working prototypes, pilots, or early commercial deployments exist, but the technology is not yet proven economical or reliable at scale.

## What it is
OTEC: generating power from the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water.

## State of the art (2026)

The island nations (for whom it matters most) and the research institutes.

Warm water evaporates a working fluid, driving a turbine; cold deep water condenses it. The plant is a heat engine running on a ~20C difference; the engineering is dominated by the giant cold-water pipe.

## Honest timeline
Small plants now; the economics work only where power is very expensive (remote islands).

demo_code:
"""Demo for "Precision-fermentation dairy": Wright's-law learning curve. Executed at build time."""

print(f"Doublings needed to reach {TARGET} {UNIT}: {need:.1f}")
assert 0 < PR < 1 and C0 > 0
